commit message:
Off-diagonal CASPT2 terms via Operator[ IL ][ IR ][ w ][ left + SIZE * right ]

 - IL is the left  center irrep as used in the overlap matrices
 - IR is the right center irrep as used in the overlap matrices
 - w is the active space orbital connecting to the fock operator (of irrep IL x IR)
 - left and right are the standard combined active space indices also used for the overlap matrices

Because there are typically way more doubly occupied / virtual orbitals than active space orbitals,
it will be more efficient to construct intermediates based on "w".

In this form, the Operators can be easily rotated the new basis which removes the overlap matrices
and diagonalizes the diagonal blocks of the CASPT2 Fock operator.

commit message:
Add files via upload

Very new to coding and this is my first "big" project in modifying a script. So welcome to 
This PBS version is modified mainly based on the LSF version, but also took other versions as reference. Main changed to create this version is build the job dependencies to guarantee the sequential steps of each job in the original juicer.sh script. #PBS -W depend=afterok:jobID headerline is used.
The launch stats steps and post processing steps are moved into two separate scripts to avoid the variable value problems (expansion) in multiple level of heredocs. These two scripts will be called from the main juicer.sh at the appropriate step.
As a summary, the follwing scripts have been modified:
juicer.sh
split_rmdups.awk
mega.sh
The following two scripts has been added (extracted from the juicer.sh)
launch_stats.sh
postprocessing.sh

All steps has been tested till the ARROWHEAD step.
*HiCCUP step has not been tested in this version because of some un-resolved error in loading Jcuda native libraries.

One important notice for successful run of this PBS version:
***The $groupname variable has to be maximally 7 characters long*****
This length may change according to your cluster setup. See below for the reason.
The jobs' dependency of this PBS version juicer is based on jobID of each step. And the jobID of each job is obtained through the qstat output based on the specific job Name, jobID_stepx= $(qstat |grep <specific job name string> |cut -c 1-7).  Unfortunately, PBS can not use job Name in building job dependency. The job Name column in qstat output has a maximum length of 16 characters by default. When the job Name exceeds this max length, the beginning part of the job Name string will be replaced by “…” and then followed by the last 13 characters (see examples below). If the job name is not fully displayed, the jobID value may be null due to the failure at grep step.  Each job Name contains the $groupname, which gives each run specific timestamp and avoid's disruption from other runs of juicer from the same user. A potential cause of this problem is the ${groupname} value being too long. I have added comments in the juicer.sh script for setting this variable. 
Below is a example of job names being too long:
$qstat
Job ID                    Name             User            Time Use S Queue
------------------------- ---------------- --------------- -------- - -----
2294690.pbs                STDIN            mzhibo          00:00:15 R batch          
2294778.pbs                make4Cbedgraph   mzhibo                 0 R batch          
2294784.pbs                ...dgraph1111111 mzhibo                 0 Q batch          
$

A complete rewrite of generate_site_positions.py

This is a complete rewrite of generate_site_positions.py.
The new version runs under python3 as well as python2.
It corrects an error found in the previous version where the very last number in the result was wrong (it was one too many).
It can work with multiple test strings at the same time (they must be enumerated in a python list).
Wildcard search (using N, M, R, W, Y, S, K, H, B, V, D) is also possible with the new algorithm.
Compared to the previous version this program runs faster for simple test strings (strings without wildcards).
The script contains a dictionary for genome/filename mappings and another one for enzyme/test string mappings which users can modify easily according to their needs.

commit message:
Major changes:
-- Fragment maps no longer included in Hi-C file by default. Before you would exclude them with the -x flag; now use -f to include.
-- dups: now have flag -j for "just exact matches"; this will only eliminate exact match duplicates. Overall this flag is not recommended. However, if you find your jobs are often getting stuck at the dedup phase, it can be because of low complexity or low mapping quality and this flag will allow the jobs to finish much faster. You will still be left with near-duplicates in your library - so use caution when interpreting results. In particular note that near-duplicates are usually machine errors, not true biological results, and thus ought to be removed.
--  Multiple ligation junctions now supported in juicer and statistics.pl script

Minor changes:
- making scripts more consistent by having check for system for juicer_tools path

commit message:
Introducing wildcard characters in test strings

This is a complete rewrite of generate_site_positions.py.
The new version runs under python3 as well as python2.
It corrects an error found in the previous version where the very last number in the result was wrong (it was one too many).
It can work with multiple test strings at the same time.
Its search algorithm uses regular expressions so wildcard symbols (N, M, R, W, Y, S, K, H, B, V, D) in test strings can also be used to find matches.
The price of using regular expressions is slower execution.
The script contains a dictionary for genome/filename mappings and another one for enzyme/test string mappings which users can modify easily according to their needs.

Bulge mass due to accreted stars is now followed

- Previously, the code was following only the mass that was formed via
starbursts due to disk instabilities and mergers. That mass is by
definition in the bulge. However, another growth channel for the bulge
is the accretion of stars that were formed in the disk of the primary
and/or secondary galaxy that because of the merger is transferred to the
bulge. This is now being followed. 

- For that it was necessary to add in the components.h a property to
track that growth channel, and galaxy_mergers was edited to explicitely
track that growth.

commit message:
New type2_galaxies_view class

This new class will allow us to directly iterate over a vector of Galaxy
objects whose type is TYPE2 but without having to create a new vector
with copies of the original Galaxy objects, and therefore enabling us to
access them by reference, and modify them as necessary. Because the
class offers being() and end() methods it means it can be used in
range-for loops, algorithms and more.

where the actual logic happens. The iterator takes the begin() and end()
of a vector of Galaxy objects. Both at creation time and after normal
increments (i.e., operator++ is called), the iterator continues
advancing through the original vector of Galaxy objects until a TYPE2
galaxy is found.

This new class will be vital when switching the Subhalos.galaxy member
from being a vector of GalaxyPtr to a vector of Galaxy objects.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Sorting data before using it

In several cases (e.g., SMF z1) the observational data will not be
necessarily sorted by X value. There is also no guarantee that the model
data will be sorted in any particular order. Although this is no problem
when plotting data or even interpolating, it makes Y data comparison and
handling invalid, as values in one array do not necessarily correspond,
after interpolation, to the values in the corresponding positions in the
other. This became apparent when trying to plot some of this data, where
one could see solid lines zig-zaging around the plotting area.

Sorting both observational and model data ensures that the resulting Y
data arrays are position-compatible, and thus makes their array-wise
calculations valid.

commit message:
Avoiding MPL bug triggered by "empty" error bars

There was a bug in matplotlib (versions 1.5.1 and 2.1.x) where error
bars that looked "empty" (in terms of them evaluating to
np.any(error_bars) == False) caused an IndexError to be raised. To avoid
this we simply don't pass down error bars that look like this from our
common.errobars method (e.g., an error bar that looks like [0, 0], which
would produce no visible output anyway), and make sure we use this
method instead of the Axes.errorbar method directly where this has been
an issue.

The version of matplotlib shipped with Ubuntu Xenial was exactly 1.5.1,
which is why we were suffering from this bug when updating to the newer
Ubuntu images in Travis.

See https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/issues/9699 for details.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Fixing compilation with OpenMP

The change introduced in 5060a37 had good intentions, but nasty
consequences: it turns out that in a few systems the
OpenMP_CXX_LIBRARIES variable could be empty, and therefore at linking
time the linker needs to be given the OpenMP flag as well. This was
happening implicitly when we were appending the OpenMP flag to the
CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS variable, so when we switched to using
add_compile_options we lost that implicit behavior, and broke
the compilation of OpenMP-enabled shark in certain situations.

The didn't present itself in any of our Travis and AppVeyor instances,
where things compiled correctly. The first platform where we saw this
was our local pleiades cluster, where we are using compilers that are
installed as modules (i.e., outside /usr and /usr/local) which probably
plays a key role on triggering this defect.

This fix doesn't fully revert 5060a37; instead it sticks to using
add_compiler_options and on top of that it adds the OpenMP flag to the
linker flags. This seems to be the accepted solution for adding linker
flags globally. An even better way of doing this of course would be to
use the LINK_FLAGS target property, but we don't use target properties
at all in shark (yet).

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Preventing errors when using shark-submit -p

When shark-submit is requested to automatically produce the standard set
of plots, the scripts that produce the plots will fail (or not)
depending on whether shark's configuration file lists the necessary
snapshots that the plots need to read as output snapshots. Instead of
simply relying on users actively adding those snapshots to the
configuration file they use to execute shark, we now make sure that the
snapshots that will be required by the plots are also listed in the
execution.output_snapshots parameter. We do this by asking the python
scripts which snapshots correspond to a particular set of redshifts
(which we know the plots need), and append the resulting list of
snapshots to the aforementioned parameter.

In the future we shouldn't even need to ask *which* redshifts are
needed, because that information is already contained somehow in the
plotting scripts themselves. When that time comes we simply need to ask
the plotting scripts which snapshots it needs, and not which snapshots
correspond to particular redshifts.

commit message:
Don't use temporary map to index halos by snapshot

The only advantage of this indexing was that it quickly returned the
full list of halos for a given snapshot, but on the other hand this is
one of the big small-living structures that increase the peak memory
usage of shark. Not using it takes that peak down a bit, which is
always a good thing.

only those for the given snapshot. Rather than using a raw loop over all
the halos, and manually filtering halos out, we use the new range_filter
class together with the new in_snapshot predicate class. These together
then take care of "automatically" iterating over the halos for which the
condition is true, plus it gives us (with an extra iteration) the size
of the range.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Switch code to use gsl_set_error_handler_off

Until now we have been using a custom GSL error handler that raises an
exception when called. This has worked well so far, but in principle is
not guaranteed to work, as C++ exceptions do not necessarily transmit
correctly through the C layer of GSL.

This commit changes the GSL error handler used by shark to be the "off"
built-in error handler. This in turn means we need to be diligent and
check the return codes of GSL function invocations, which we do with our
new gsl_invoke function. Since our function turns error codes into
gsl_error exceptions the rest of the code doesn't need much change.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Implement PSO state dumping/loading

This is a first implementation that is very barebones, but works: it
keeps track of the last version of the PSO internal state (best
particle/swarm positions and values, plus all particle positions and
velocities), which are dumped at the end of each iteration into a file.
When the PSO is loaded we check for the existence of this file, and if
found we then load the PSO state from there instead of creating one from
scratch. The state includes the last successful PSO iteration that was
run, which we use to start the main loop.

Note that some other state is not kept. For instance, all user-provided
options are discarded, and therefore users must still use the same
command line they used in a previous run to make sense of things.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Don't use temporary map to index halos by ID

Just like the other map we used to index halos by snapshot, the only
advantage of this one was that it quickly returned the halo for any
corresponding ID, while on the other hand this increased the peak memory
usage of shark. Not using this map removes the last peak we had in
memory usage, and is the final stepping stone in reducing the maximum
memory footprint of shark by ~20%.

The alternative now is to first sort the given halos by ID, and then use
a binary search to look for any given one. In practice this seems to be
yielding similar runtimes, but we can even tolerate some performance
degradation in favour of a lower memory footprint.

For the time being the sort_by_id and find_by_id functions are sitting
statically in the tree_builder module, but I have a local version of
these fully generalized for all shark component types, including pointer
types, which would be useful if needed in the future to avoid code
repetition.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
New OpenMP-related utilities header file

This header file contains two functions: omp_static_for and
omp_dynamic_for. These are templated, and represent the two types of
OpenMP for loops we have been using until now. They use either a
[start,end) integer range over which parallelization should occur, or a
container supporting random iterators which is then looped from
[0,size). In both cases a callable is provided that should be called
with individual elements coming out from the iteration.

Passing down the full container instead of first/last iterators is
necessary if we want to support older OpenMP versions. Only in OpenMP
3.0 one can pass a random iterator to the loop construct; before that
the variable in the loop construct could only be an integer.

commit message:
Better packing for Subhalo/Galaxy classes

The order in which the members of these two classes were defined has
been quite organic until now. This has led to an inefficient packing of
data within the structure, as additional padding was being inserted in
some places due to the alignment requirements of the different data
types.

In this commit we are improving the packing of members on these two
classes by performing the two more basic optimizations we can do: bring
all those of the same type together, and putting those of bigger size
first. By doing so the size of the Subhalo class (with gcc 8) went down
from 360 to 352 bytes, while Galaxy remained the same.

Since we were rearranging the members within the class, I also took the

documentation.

commit message:
clang-tidy: more override, less virtual

These were highlighted by the modernize-use-override check. On the one
hand using virtual on member function declarations that are not the
initial one is not necessary, while on the other using the override
keyword forces the compiler to fail if the function is not an actual
override of a virtual function. Therefore, using the latter instead of
the former is the best approach.

Using this I actually found that one of the functions that were
overriden in the PhysicalModel class was not declared virtual. However,
since the compiler could see it when compiling the derived class, it
still generated the correct code.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
OMP-aware galaxy creation

Creating galaxies for the different MergerTrees within the same threads
that are going to process them should help be more NUMA-friendly, as the

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
More informative messages on runtime performance

This commit adds the collection of more fine-grained information about
evolution times. This information is designed to give us a better
understanding on how parallelism is working in current and future
executions.

Firstly, we are now storing per-thread timing information, such that we
can display at the end how much time each thread spent on which task
during galaxy evolution. These numbers should be as equal as possible
across threads, which in turn would should a good spread of
computational load. We previously had this information available, but
only in a per-snapshot basis. With this new dimension we can show
aggregates on a per-snapshot or per-thread basis, plus totals for each
as well. The final report on total times is coded as a separate, public
method to allow in the future to print it from outside (e.g., a signal
handler).

Secondly, I'm adding an "evolution rate" statistic on a per-snapshot
level; that is how long it takes to evolve each galaxy. Locally I get
something in the order of tens of microseconds per galaxy, which a good
starting point for comparing different systems and executions, specially
when running with different number of threads.

Finally, a total "evolution walltime" is also calculated and shown at
the end of each shark execution. This is the final number we care about
shrinking when doing parallelism, so it's handy to have it readily
available for inspection and comparison.

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

commit message:
Implementing lenient galaxy equality checks

Instead of always asserting over the values read from the HDF5 file
directly for full equality, we now support first sorting them, and then
asserting that they are "close enough" (both in relative and absolute
terms). This type of equality check is useful for when, for some reason,
we change for example the order in which different structures (halos,
subhalos, galaxies) are looped over, and thus their appearance on the
output files. Changing that order can also in turn affect other values
computed by shark, because floating point is not necessarily
associative/commutative; therefore some difference can be tolerated in
the values themselves.

The default is still to check for full equality, but the new
-l/--lenient command-line flag allows for the new check variant to be
used.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Stopping usage of std::shared_ptr<Galaxy>

While using std::shared_ptr<Galaxy> was convenient as they can be easily
copied, but other than this it doesn't give us any benefit, as Galaxy
objects are always owned by a single Subhalo and referenced only
internally by Subhalos; i.e., there are no other objects holding
references galaxies contained in a Subhalo.

On top of this, two drawbacks could be also observed. The first is that
used std::shared_ptr means we need extra memory to hold the pointer
objects themselves. This amounted to a fairly small number compared to
the size of the Galaxy objects themselves, but was still unnecessary
memory usage. The second, and main, drawback was that access to Galaxy
objects always occurred through one level of memory indirection, which
would certainly not help much the cache system when looping through a
collection of galaxies, as they would not be contiguous in memory.

The change from using std::shared_ptr<Galaxy> to using Galaxy directly
in the codebase is fairly big, and considers the following aspects:

 * The main GalaxyPtr type alias is now defined as "Galaxy *" rather
than std::shared_ptr<Galaxy>

 * The Subhalo::galaxies member is now a std::vector<Galaxy> instead of
a std::vector<Galaxy *>. As a result of this change all the code
iterating over this member in range-for loops had to be ported to refer
to galaxy members via . instead of -> (e.g.; in "for (auto &galaxy:
subhalo->galaxies) { galaxy->sfr_disk = 0; }" galaxy->sfr_disk had to be
replaced by galaxy.sfr_disk).

 * The change above affected also a number of functions that previously
received GalaxyPtr objects by reference. Since we changed those to
receive Galaxy references now, we took the chance to make sure we pass
constant references when possible.

 * The central_galaxy and type1_galaxy methods still return a GalaxyPtr,
as some Subhalos are allowed to lack a central or type2 galaxy. Callers
of these methods don't need to change though, since using a "Galaxy *"
object and a std::shared_ptr<Galaxy> object is very similar.

 * To accommodate for const-correctness, a const version of the two
methods above has also been added. These return a ConstGalaxyPtr (i.e.,
"const Galaxy *").

 * The type2_galaxies method of the Subhalo class needed a bit
refurbishment, most of which was contained in an earlier commit.
Previously this method returned a newly-created vector with copies of
the GalaxyPtr objects contained in the Subhalo::galaxies member that
were of type2. Because the std::shared_ptr copies referred to the same
underlying Galaxy object they could be safely used to modify the latter,
and some code relied on this. Now that we store Galaxy objects directly
this vector-of-copies behavior doesn't satisfy this requirement anymore,
and therefore we are switching to return a type2_galaxies_view object
instead. This object allows users to iterate over the Galaxy objects
contained in the Subhalo::galaxies vector, return references to them,
but skipping those that are not type2.

 * To easily get the total number of type2 galaxies a new
type2_galaxies_count() method has been added to Subhalo.

 * The transfer_galaxies* methods in Subhalo have been reworked to avoid
copies. As a consequence the copy_galaxies_to method hhas been removed,
and the remove_galaxies() method's signature has been changed.

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
nfw_distribution overhauled

The nfw_distribution class (previously known as NfwDistribution) now
lives in its own header file, so it can be easily imported from more
modules without pulling the entire dark_matter_halos header file.

nfw_distribution also follows RandomNumberDistribution.
RandomNumberDistribution is a C++11 concept with a number of
requirements. Most of these we don't actually need (we actually only
need the () operator), but having them all makes it easier for other
people to reuse this code, or even put it somewhere standing on its own
right.

This improved implementation has also two main advantages over the
original: first, it is templated on the floating point type that it
uses, so it can be used with types other than double (although we
internally still use only the double type). Secondly, and more
importantly, it doesn't internally use the gsl_sf_lambert_W0 function
anymore, therefore dropping this requirement on potential users.
Instead, users need to specialize the lambert_w0 struct for the required
floating point type, and provide an () operator that returns the value
of the Lambert W0 function for a given input. Later in the code we then
specialize the lambert_w0 struct for doubles using the gsl function.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Create initial galaxies in bulk

Initial galaxies are created in "starting" central subhalos (i.e.,
those that don't have ascendants). This process was previously done
inside the halo/subhalo/galaxy evolution loop, and therefore galaxies
were being created when the corresponding Halo was being evaluated.
On the other hand the subhalo merging logic requires all central
subhalos to be properly populated with galaxies. Thus, depending on the
looping order, the subhalo merging logic could fail (because it finds a
"starting" central subhalo that has not been evaluated yet, and hasn't
had its galaxies created).

To solve this issue we now create all initial galaxies in all "starting"
central subhalos across all snapshots. This ensures that later during
the evolution loop we will always find galaxies in central subhalos.
This logic has been put into a separate class, where it is efficiently
called and logged.

commit message:
Improving OpenMP version checking

OpenMP support across the 3.x series of cmake has varied a bit, reflecting the
needs of different compilers. In particular, Intel compilers' support for
OpenMP was not being correctly recognized, as additional linkage needs to
happen to create a fully working OpenMP program, which wasn't being catered for
in our manual test compilation for version checking.

recognition when available, also adding the required OpenMP libraries to
the linking process of shark to ensure a successful build. When we find
the particular situation of an Intel compiler failing to find OpenMP
support with cmake < 3.9 then we also display a message to the user to

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Datasets of different size are unequal

So far we have used compare_galaxies.py automatically to determine
whether the output of two very similar shark executions are equal or
not. When the are *not* equal we have been lucky in that the number of
galaxies on each hdf5 file have been the same, but this doesn't need to
be true: the stochastic nature of the code will eventually produce
slightly different number of galaxies due to mergers happening or not
depending on other factors. This in turn means that when comparing two
hdf5 files we need to first check the shape of the datasets under the
galaxies/ group before proceeding any further, and if the datasets have
different shapes then we consider the two files not being equal.

Note that although this fixes an spurious error we suffered in our
automatic tests, it also is a good idea on its own, as the script can
now compare arbitrarily different outputs from wildly different runs and
mark them as being different.

commit message:
Modified AGN feedback jet mode memory model

The original model in Lagos et al. (2024, SHARK v2.0) adopted the
model of Croton et all (2016), which estipulated that the heating radius
maintained a memory and could only increase in size.

This was made more flexible by including a redshift below which
the memory if the heating radius in turned on. The idea behind is that
the high-z universe is very dynamic and halos can go on and off
hydrostatic equilibrium, while at lower redshifts this stabilises
and halos can remain on hydrostatic eq. The redshift at which
that transition happens was added as a free parameter.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
ODESolver redesigned for better memory allocation

Originally, ODESolver was designed to evolve an ODE system with a fixed
set of initial conditions through different time steps using a single
object. However, the way PhysicalModel uses the solver is different: it
evolves an ODE system for different sets of initial conditions through
the same period of time. Therefore, the only way to fit the old design
of ODESolver into how PhysicalModel used it was to create a new
ODESolver for each initial condition set (i.e., each galaxy) and evolve
it a single step of delta_t. This situation was obviously not ideal, as
it introduces unnecessary dynamic memory allocation/deallocation for
*each* galaxy that is being evolved.

The new design of ODESolver fits better into the way it ends up being
used. It is initially created with a reference to the ODE system that
will be used throughout but without initial conditions; on the other
hand, the evolve method receives each time the initial conditions, a
delta_t parameter, and the ODE system is reset and then evolved for the
given parameters. This new design then dynamically allocates only one
set of objects for the lifetime of a PhysicalModel, improving the
behavior of shark in multi-threading situations.

Also in this commit we are taking the opportunity to add a deleter class
for the gsl_odeiv2_driver object. This makes the code easier to
maintain, as we now have both a move constructor and an assignment
operator implicitly declared.

author: clagos <claudia.lagos@icrar.org>
commit message:
New model of stellar tidal stripping implemented

This new model is based on the calculations of Errani et al. (2015),
which modelled the tidal stripping of satellite galaxies in a Milky-Way
halo. The outcome of the simulations were fit and here I adopt the best
fit for a cuspy core with an r_star/a=0.1. This seems to have the
desired effect on the stellar mass function.

There is a free parameter which is the minimum allowed threshold of
virial mass ratio (Mvir,now/Mvir,infall), which is relevant for galaxies
that go from centrals to becoming type II without ever becoming type 1.
If the more normal scenario of central->type I->type II takes place,
then tidal stripping is more gradual (as it depends on the virial mass
loss).

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
MergerTree holding Halos in vector, not map

The indexing of HaloPtr objects by snapshot as done until now adds to
the overall memory consumption because (at least in gcc and clang) a
std::map<int, HaloPtr> is bigger than a std::vector<HaloPtr> in size.

Instead of indexing by snapshot and using more memory, we are now saving
them directly into a vector. In order to still satisfy the API needs of
MergerTree (i.e., get all halos in a given snapshot, and get the root
halo of the treee) we are using two techniques. Firstly, for efficiently
getting all halos in a snapshot we are "consolidating" a merger tree
after it has been fully populated with halos, which translates to
sorting its halos by snapshot; later when users requests halos in an
arbitrary snapshot we binary search the begin/end of the subrange on the
vector containing halos at the requested snapshot and return that as a
range object which can be looped through. This "consolidation" step is
important, as without it we would need search for halos in the entire
vector with linear complexity instead of logarithmic.

Secondly, to offer the roots of the merger tree as a range-like object
we are reusing the range_filter class with the appropriate filter
object. This still required linear complexity, but it's a much rarer
operation, and was linear before too.

This refactoring means we also don't need the static NONE member, so we
can actually remove the merger_tree.cpp file altogether.

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Support for multi-threaded reproducible runs

The way we aim to support multi-threaded reproducible runs is by seeding
the RNG with a object-dependent value before using them to draw values
from the different distributions. This re-seeding, combined with the
fact that we use the ID of the particular object the operation is
related to, means the values drawn from the distributions don't depend
on the order in which we invoke the operations anymore; instead, they
now depend on the initial seed (which is potentially set by the user)
and the object being operated on.

This change means that storing the RNG as a member of the classes that
used them is no longer necessary, and it can actually be detrimental
when classes are shared by different threads, like in the case of the
DarkMatterHaloes base class. To avoid race conditions we thus simply

distributions, seeding it with the correct value right at construction

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Initial OpenMP parallelization

The easiest way to parallelize shark is to process merger trees in
parallel. Merger trees are (currently) fully independent of each other,
so in principle they can be processed in parallel without any side
effects.

The number of threads is a user-provided parameters. This makes the
number of threads more explicit in the code, instead of relying in the
OMP_NUM_THREADS environment variables or other implicit ways of defining
the number of threads to use. However, we still give users the ability
to use whatever default the OpenMP implementation gives by specifying
"-t 0".

To properly run things in parallel we need to make sure we don't share
state across threads. The main stateful objects at the moment are the
GSL ODE system and the GSL integrator, and any class that directly and
indirectly uses them. We thus are now creating multiple copies of all
these objects as necessary. When the code is compiled without OpenMP
support a single copy of these objects is created, but the overall code
is still generic and assumes there is always a collection of such
objects.

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

commit message:
Improving OpenMP version checking

OpenMP support across the 3.x series of cmake has varied a bit, reflecting the
needs of different compilers. In particular, Intel compilers' support for
OpenMP was not being correctly recognized, as additional linkage needs to
happen to create a fully working OpenMP program, which wasn't being catered for
in our manual test compilation for version checking.

With this commit we are using the newer support for OpenMP version
recognition when available, also adding the required OpenMP libraries to
the linking process of shark to ensure a successful build. When we find
the particular situation of an Intel compiler failing to find OpenMP
support with cmake < 3.9 then we also display a message to the user to
let them know they should try with a newer cmake version.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
numerical_constants fashion emergency

This is a big change, but mostly cosmetic.

First of all there was a big number of constants defined in the
shark::constants namespace that were not used: those are gone.

Secondly, the description of each constant was usually in the same line
as the declaration itself, while now they are properly formatted as
doxygen docs; moreover, each logical group of constants is under a @name
tag as well.

And last but not least, all constants are now defined with type double.
There was no particular reason for using floats in the first place, and
actually a few reasons not to: firstly, outside the constants namespace
we do all (or almost all) our calculations using doubles, so these
constant values were being implicitly promoted to doubles; secondly, the
calculation of the constants themselves was using float numbers with
wide dynamical ranges, and therefore might have created unnecessarily
incorrect constant values (but I didn't double check this), even if they
were being promoted to doubles. And finally, because literal decimal
values in C++ are doubles (unless they have an 'f' suffix) it would have
required a big amount of effort to safely declare those literals as
floats without having warnings in some compilers about literal value
truncations (MSVC was particularly noisy about that).

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Parallelising calculation of molecular gas

The usual drill takes place: per-thread copies of the required objects
are created, and aggregation happens at the end of the parallel block.
In this case we need to keep track of per-thread molgas_per_galaxy
objects, plus a StarFormation object for each thread to avoid shared
state.

This is the final major parallelisation point we needed to address
during the main evolution loop; after this the time spent in parallel
sections accounts for ~90% of the wall time in common cases measured so
far. After, parallelising more of the initial data loading and
verification procedures is the next main goal, but we are already in a
pretty good state.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Multiple volumes not always to "multiple_batches"

In general, the directory structure for outputs coming from shark has
the form "<output-base>/<simulation>/<model>/<snapshot>/<subvolume>". On
the other hand, a single shark instance can process multiple subvolumes.
In these cases the <subvolume> part of the directory structure is
hardcoded to be "multiple_batches".

In the case of PSO runs with multiple subvolumes, we effectively end up
running shark instances using several subvolumes each, and therefore we
expect the "multiple_batches" directory to be present. This continues to
be true, but in preparation for "offline evaluation" of existing results
we need to take into account outputs coming not from a PSO run, but from
other executions (HPC submissions, manual runs). In those cases,
specially in the HPC case, we probably ran shark separately for each
subvolume, generating separate <subvolume> directories, which we *don't*
want to internally translate to "multiple_batches".

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Making PSO job monitoring more precise

Previously, after our PSO logic submitted a job to the queue we used the
job name (which we create) to check whether the job had finished or not.
This had the disadvantage of getting confused when two people were
running a PSO optimization in the same cluster, as they would end up
with similar job names at some point (we actually experienced this!).
This caused the PSO logic of a person A to wait for the jobs of the
another person B to complete, even if A's job had completed.

By using the new ability of shark-submit to report the underlying job ID
through the stdout we now catch that information and monitor that
specific job.

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Use Galaxy to prime random orbit's seed values

When we introduced the thread-safe random number generation changes a
few months back we wrongly assumed that using a Halo's ID to prime the
seed number used to generate galaxy's orbit values was correct. It
actually wasn't: it has the effect that for all Galaxies in the same
Halo the same seed is generated, and therefore the same orbital values
are generated.

This commit adds a Galaxy parameter to the generate_random_orbits call
so that it can be used to prime the random number generator's seed
instead of the Halo. This should ensure results are different across
Galaxies even when they belong to the same Halo.

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Avoid race conditions with random distributions

Both the lognormal and the uniform distributions used by the
DarkMatterHalos class (which is shared by multiple threads) do not have
any guarantee of being thread-safe, and indeed gcc's implementation of
the normal distribution keeps some state. This creates race conditions
between multiple threads that might be using them at the same time.

To avoid these race conditions we don't store the distributions objects
anymore as members of DarkMatterHalos, but create them from scratch each
time we need them. This shouldn't be an expensive operation, as neither
of them does calculations at construction time; but even if they did
they would probably be minor compared to the rest of the computations we
do in shark.

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Fix optim for local usage and enhance performance

The version of optim that runs shark locally was not working correctly:
it spawned multiple shark instances for each of the particles, but the
evaluation of the results was not done centrally. On top of this,
several bits and pieces of logic were misaligned with respect to the HPC
version, which as seen more use and therefore is better maintained.

This commit fixes how we run shark PSO locally. Instead of letting the
pso module invoke the optimisation function N times, we now follow a
similar strategy to the HPC case: we ask pso to issue a single call to
the optimisation function with all the particular, and within our
function we use a multiprocessing pool to run the individual shark
instances and collect the results.

Thanks to this change, the code to collect results after shark instances
have been run can be shared between the hpc and non-hpc mode. In fact,
at the top level we now always pass the same evaluation function to pso,
and then internally we switch between hpc and non-hpc only to spawn the
shark instances, with the rest of the code being common to both cases.

On top of that, I've also taken the opportunity to improve how results
are calculated and gathered. Because now we handle our own
multiprocessing pool, we are using it too to collect the results for
each particle in parallel, which makes a big difference in speed.
Additionally, the way we collected the model and error values for each
constraint evaluation was unnecessarily re-evaluating each constraint
each time, adding up to the processing times, so that has been now been
fixed.

There still remains an issue with how model and error values are stored
into a file for future usage. This has accidentally worked in the past
because there has only been a single constraint, or all the given
constrains result in module and error arrays with the same amount of
values. This isn't the case in general though, as running with
constraints that produce different amount of model/error values can
result in heterogeneous array shapes that cannot be represented as-is
with numpy, and thus don't work with the current code. To remain
backwards-compatible I've kept the code that does the dumping of these
files, but added a try/catch block around it to warn users if these
values couldn't be saved. In the future we should fix this.

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Creating more balanced partitions of merger trees

Until now the way we distribute workload across our OpenMP threads is by
simply assigning different chunks of merger trees to each thread in a
static fashion. This is a good strategy if the workload is similar
across all threads; otherwise the parallel for loop is as fast as the
slowest thread with more workload.

It turns out that odds are not necessarily in our favour, and in average
merger trees are not equally loaded with galaxies, which restricts our
parallelism. To overcome this we manually partition the list of merger
trees based on their galaxy count using a simple greedy algorithm,
producing partitions with roughly the same amount of galaxies, hence
spreading the workload better across OpenMP threads.

Initial experiments show an improvement in the walltime, with scaling
now going up to ~10x when running mini-surfs with 20 threads (it was
~<8x before). Note that galaxies live in a specific snapshot at a time,
so maybe we could study doing merger tree partitioning once per
snapshot, which should give more accurate results; this has the downside
however of being potentially more expensive in the long run, so
pros/cons would have to be weighted and compared.

Other than the partitioning itself, the other main aspect that had to be
taken care of is the fact that, without proper care, elements would have
been written out to the output files in different orders depending on
the amount of threads used by the execution. This breaks our rule of
staying reproducible and thus had to be dealt with appropriately by
sorting the halos to be written by ID to ensure the same order
regardless of how they were processed.

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

commit message:
Convert mem-per-task to mem-per-cpu

This wasn't a problem in the days when we supported only single-threaded shark
instances, but now that we support multi-threaded instances, and we allow users
to specify a number of CPUs to use per instance via -c, we need to scale the
memory per task/instance so it takes into account that more than one CPU is
used per task.

For example, when using "-V 0 -c 16 -m 10g" (i.e., a single instance to process
subvolume 0 using 16 cores and 10g of memory) we were requesting 160g of memory
(10g per CPU). We now scale this value correctly, and ask the correct amount
(640m per CPU = 10g per task).

author: clagos <clagos@anita-II>
commit message:
Changes to appropriately account for angular momentum evolution.

Several changes have been included to appropriately account for the
angular momentum evolution in galaxy components gas and disk:

- new parameters included to allow for angular momentum internal
calculation within disks and bulges.

- ODEs in physical model have been extended to include the equations
that follow the angular momentum exchange between components.

- Whether we assume stars form from the same sAM of the gas, or we allow
for the molecular gas to pass that information into the stellar
component, is encoded in star_formation*

- We now follow the specific angular momentum of the hot and cold halo
components.

- New functions of angular momentum of the disk, bulge and halo were
included in dark_matter_halos. All of the angular momentum functions are
within dark_matter_halos and star_formation.

- Galaxy mergers, gas cooling and disk instabilities were modified
accordingly to take into account these new functions. 

- Stellar feedback was also modified to allow for possible outflows with
preferential angular momentum losses. The standard shark model works
assuming that outflows carry out the same specific angular momentum than
the gas in the disk-bulge, but can could be modified in the future.

- There are still problems with (i) the bulge sizes and how to calculate
them during minor mergers, (ii) how I'm calculating jrate in the case
where jgas is assumed to be constant, as this should return a jgas after
the solution of the ODEs that is the same as when it started, but for
some reason that is not happening. This needs to be solved.

When building the trees and making connections subhalo-descendant, if there is a transient in the descendant halo and several constraints are fulfilled, then default subhalo-descendant connection is broken and a subhalo-transient connection has priority. author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Re-implementing all_subhalos using subhalos_view

The change was almost transparent, with some exceptions which I describe
below.

First, the code defining the central subhalo for each Halo was relying
on the first element of all_subhalos() being the most massive. We do
this explicitly now for this specific case. This same code was also
relying on all_subhalos() returning new SubhaloPtr objects, so it could
safely remove the satellite subhalo from the underlying
Halo::satellite_subhalos vector and still keep using it. This isn't the
case now though: the subhalos_view object returns direct references to
the underlying vector, so once a satellite is removed from the vector
the SubhaloPtr isn't valid anymore (most of the times, unless someone
else is pointing to it). The solution is obviously to make a copy on
this case.

The other exception was the code performing the linking between
snapshots, which removes subhalos *while iterating over them*. This
worked before because we always returned a new vector, and therefore
removing subhalos from the Halo had no effect on the iteration over the
vector. We explicitly create a new vector for this iteration now, which
then makes the code happy.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Make user-provided evaluation function GSL-safe

Until now we have always given the GSL ODE solver driver C++ functions
that can actually throw exceptions. These exceptions might or might not
make it through the C stack of GSL (depending on compilers and
compilation flags) and therefore cannot be considered a safe way of
handling errors.

This commit creates a thin wrapper around the C++ user-provided
ODE evaluation functions to catch any exceptions and turning them into
GSL error codes. This is done in such a way that user-provided functions
don't need to care about GSL error codes, and can happily continue to
throw exceptions.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Delaying the transfer of galaxies across snapshots

Galaxies were being transferred from a Subhalo to its descendant Subhalo
in two different places in the code. The first location was at the end
of the per-halo evolution loop via galaxy_mergers.merging_subhalos, and
the second was at the end of the per-snapshot evolution loop via
transfer_galaxies_to_next_snapshot. In between (i.e., after the per-halo
loop finished, but before the per-snapshot loop iteration finished) the
track_total_baryons function was assuming all galaxies were still living
in the current snapshot, and therefore it failed to create a history
item for those that had been transferred to the next snapshot already.

This change delayes the transfer *in the time dimension* of those
galaxies so it always happens at the end of iteration of the
per-snapshot evolution loop. This ensures that the total baryon mass
tracking, and other bits of logic that might depend on snapshot-local
data, can reach all galaxies living in the current snapshot before they
are transferred to the next.

Note that the galaxy_mergers.merging_subhalos function still performs
galaxy transfers when merging subhalos, but this is across subhalos that
are part of the same halo, and therefore they do not move across
snapshots.

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Make user-provided integration function GSL-safe

Just like in the case of the GSL ODE solver, until now we have always
given the GSL integration routines C++ functions for it to integrate.
These function can actually throw exception, but those exceptions might
or might not make it through the C stack of GSL (depending on compilers
and compilation flags) and therefore cannot be considered a safe way of
handling errors.

This commit creates a thin wrapper around the C++ user-provided
integration functions to catch any exceptions, turning them into GSL
error codes. This is not possible directly, as functions to be
integrated by GSL don't have a way to signal any internal errors. We
thus not only return NaN on failures, but also keep track ourselves of
errors and check for them even after a successful GSL invocation.

These changes are done in such a way that user-provided functions don't
need to care about GSL error codes, and can happily continue to throw
exceptions.

commit message:
Define massive transients inside the code

Massive transient catalogues are not required right noe. The massive transients are flagged inside the code as the subhalos that belong to main branches that are born with an unexpectedly high number of particles: 1. find the subhalos with no main progenitor, 2. find subhalos with no progenitor that belong to main branches, 3. they are defined as transients if the particle number at birth is above the considered threshold. There are 3 different threshold in the particle number at birth for main branches: a constant value of 200 particles, a constant value of 10 times the minimum particle number for a subhalo, and 3 times the standard deviation of the particle number at birth for main branches at each snapshot. Set as a default the 3 sigma method.

Using the new redshift table

Different plotting scripts had different ways of specifying snapshots
previously: either they hardcoded the list of snapshots representing a
list of hardcoded redshifts, or they accepted a snapshot as a

list of redshifts, and calculate the snapshots from it. In the second
case we don't use the "snapshot" command-line argument anymore, but
hardcode a redshift 0 in the code, and request the corresponding
snapshot from the redshift table.

Because the "snapshot" "snapshot" positional parameter is now
unnecessary we also remove from the command-line parsing.

specify a hardcoded snapshot anymore.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Using std::vector to store subhalos in Halo

The only advantage of using a std::set over a std::vector to store the
Subhalo objects within a Halo was in being able to quickly check if a
Subhalo was already in the set; on the other hand using a std::set had a
big cost in memory: with gcc 8 and clang 7 it uses 48 bytes of memory,
compared to the 24 bytes of a vector. Thus, by using a vector we are
shoving off 24 bytes off the Halo class, which previously stood at 200
bytes in these two compilers.

In reality Halos have very few Subhalos within them, so using a vector
and then looking ourselves and finding out if a Subhalo was already part
of the Halo or not is not too costly, even though it was linear
complexity. On top of that we do this only once at Halo/Subhalo
construction time.

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Avoid copies of Halo in ascendants and merger tree

When linking Subhalos to establish their parentage relationship, we also
relate their corresponding Halos. However, due to the multiplicity
between Subhalos and Halos (one Halo contains zero or more Subhalos), we
were running the same relationship establishment logic for two Halos more than once.

This situation happened if two Subhalos SH1 and SH2, living in Halo H1,
were deemed as ascendants of Subhalos SH3 and SH4 respectively, both of
which live in Halo H2. In this case, when establishing
SH1-is-parent-of-SH3 we also established H1-is-parent-of-H2, and
repeated this operation when establishing SH2-is-parent-of-SH4, leading
finally to repeated references to H1 in the merger tree and in the list
of ascendants of H2.

recently-introduced type2_galaxies_view class. After playing with
types2_galaxies_view a bit and trying to save more memory usage in some

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Reimplement all_subhalos using all_subhalos_view

The change was almost transparent, with some exceptions which I describe
below.

First, the code defining the central subhalo for each Halo was relying
on the first element of all_subhalos() being the most massive, which
isn't the case anymore. We do this explicitly now for this specific
case. This same code was also relying on all_subhalos() returning new
SubhaloPtr objects, so it could safely remove the satellite subhalo from
the underlying Halo::satellite_subhalos vector and still keep using it.
This isn't the case now either: the all_subhalos_view object returns
direct references to the underlying vector, so once a satellite is
removed from the vector the SubhaloPtr isn't valid anymore (most of the
times, unless someone else is pointing to it). The solution is obviously
to make a copy on this case.

The other exception was the code performing the linking between
snapshots, which removes subhalos *while iterating over them*. This
worked before because we always returned a new vector, and therefore
removing subhalos from the Halo had no effect on the iteration over the
vector. We explicitly create a new vector for this iteration now, which
then makes the code happy.

A set of unit tests also demonstrates the new functionality is working
as intended in all the possible use cases.

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
Clarifying how evolution through snapshots works

This change should not affect behavior at all. It simply clarifies both
in the code in the form of comments, and in the logs in the form of more
informative text, how the process of evolving galaxies works for a given
snapshot. Because we evolve using a single snapshot number (say, "i"),
it's easy to think that we evolve AT snapshot "i", while in reality we
evolve FROM snapshot "i" to snapshot "i+1". This means that the main
evolution loop goes through the range [min, max) (i.e., open ended in
max), and that when we write galaxies (after evolution) they logically
are in snapshot "i+1".

In the case of the writing of galaxies, this "i+1" was permeating out
from the main logic loop in shark_runner and into the galaxy_writer
module (and actually only for the HDF5 writer, and not in the ASCII
writer). I've changed this so now the galaxy_writer module doesn't have
to bother with these details.

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

Check redshift data is correct

different consecutive snapshots. This caused errors down the line,
specifically because the delta_t for those snapshots was zero, which did
not play well with the GSL ODE solver of course. Depending on which
snapshots are affected, this error can appear either very quickly or
rather late during the execution of shark, which can be frustrating
during long runs.

This additional check gives a clear error message regarding the cause of
the failure, and makes shark fail quickly at startup instead of doing it
later during the main execution of the program.

author: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>
commit message:
New galaxy composition check methods

Both type of Subhalos (i.e., central and satellite) are meant to meet
certain criteria in terms of the types of galaxies that are allowed to
be contained within. Some of these checks were being performed in some
parts of the code, but not only there was some code duplication here and
there, but also checks were not being ran consistently.

This commit centralises the logic of checking that the galaxy
composition of both central and satellite subhalos meets the expected
conditions, throwing an exception if a particular situation is not met.
There are three different methods to performs checks on whatever type a
given subhalo happens to be, and to performs checks with a particular
type of subhalo in mind (therefore additionally checking that the
subhalo is of the expected type). We use these new checks throughout the
code in the place where we previously had checks, and in other new
places where we think it makes sense to check these constrains.

commit message:
Add the LOBPCG algorithm

(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LOBPCG)
Is a great method for large sparse eigenproblems. You can find a description in the file

The convergence speed depends basically on 3 factors:
- How well a preconditioner was chosen
- How well relatively separated the seeking eigenvalues are from the rest of the eigenvalues
- How well conditioned the problem is

commit message:
Low-rank DMD: Optimal solution in poylnomial time (#87)

* Implementation of the optimal closed-form DMD solution

- Added a predict function following the sklearn API.

* Added Tutorial 8 (Rough sketch)

- Added a tutorial comparing the performances of the various DMD implementations.

* Added `predict` to DMD.

- Added a `predict` function to the DMD estimator.

* Clean-ish implementation of the algorithm by Héas & Herzet

* Store the singular value of the low-dimensional DMD operator into self._svds.

* Change default DMD-operator factorization to EVD instead of SVD.

* Added Module DocString.

* Change pinv for a more efficient implementation

- Added an implementation of pseudo inverse computation dedicated to diagonal matrix. More efficient for this particular task than calling the general-purpose scipy.linalg.pinv.

- Implemented `_buiild_lowrank_op` and `_eig_from_lowrank_op` for consistency with the other DMD objects available in PyDMD.

- Sketched `_compute_amplitude` and `dynamics` for future implementation.

- Added basic tests for the current implementation of OptDMD. Note that it still misses a few functionalities that cannot hence be tested yet.

* Added optdmd to the __all__

* Remove super().__init__() for python 2/3 compatibility.

* Modified the test for atilde

- DMD and OptDMD construct slightly different low-dimensional DMD operators. The eigenvalues should be the same however.

Add exception for MemoryError in mrDMD reconstruction

When the size of the snapshot matrix is big and the number of resolution levels in mrDMD is large, a MemoryError may occur.
This happens because all partial reconstructed data are stored in the buffer before doing the summation. Although being fast, this procedure can present memory limitations.
In order to circumvent this problem, an exception for MemoryError was implemented, in which the partial data is successively added up through an explicit loop.

commit message:
Fix bug in mrDMD reconstruction due to null eigenvalues

When choosing a large number of resolution levels, the upper bins could not fit in the tree structure. In order to handle this situation, the previous implementation forced the DMD modes, amplitudes, eigenvalues, Atilda, etc. of such upper (non fitting) bins to be zero. This was done through a `try...except` statement. However, this solution was causing a problem of division by zero during the reconstruction of the dynamics. In the present commit, a threshold for the maximum resolution level was stabilished, thus eliminating the division by zero issue.
